title: Protect an unheated house
summary: Keep any heat you have at 55°F (13°C) or more and let faucets drip. If the house will freeze, shut the main valve and drain the water system, toilets, traps and water heater before the pipes freeze. Keep stored water and canned food from freezing. Watch the roof under heavy snow.
doFirst: Still have some heat? For the pipes, keep it at 55°F (13°C) or higher (people need more: see Stay warm when the heat is out), open the cabinet doors under sinks, and if water is still running, let faucets drip (New York State Department of Health, Red Cross, CDC).
Heat off in freezing weather? Save the water first, then shut the main water valve, or the well pump if it is in the house, and drain the system before the pipes freeze (Purdue Extension).
Never thaw pipes with a torch, a kerosene or propane heater, a charcoal stove or any open flame (Red Cross, CDC).
Roof sagging, creaking or cracking, or doors that suddenly stick? Get everyone out (FEMA).

blocks.p: Water expands as it freezes, and the ice can break even strong pipes (Red Cross). Pipes most at risk: outdoor hose faucets, and water pipes in unheated basements, crawl spaces, attics and garages, under kitchen cabinets, and against outside walls with little insulation (Red Cross).

list: Keep the heat on and no lower than 55°F (13°C) (New York State Department of Health; Red Cross, for a house left empty). Keep the same setting day and night (Red Cross).
Let the faucets on exposed pipes drip (CDC, New York State Department of Health). Running water through a pipe, even a trickle, helps keep it from freezing (Red Cross).
Open kitchen and bathroom cabinet doors so warm air reaches the pipes (Red Cross, New York State Department of Health, CDC). Move cleaners and chemicals out of children’s reach (Red Cross).
Keep garage doors closed if water pipes run through the garage (Red Cross).
Insulate both hot and cold water pipes in unheated areas and along outside walls (Red Cross, CDC).

blocks.p: When the house will be without heat in freezing weather, first save the water in the pipes, the water heater and the toilet tanks, then drain the system. The steps are in Water already in your house and Water in winter.
Purdue Extension adds these to the steps in Water in winter:

list: To drain the whole system, disconnect pipe unions or joints as close to the main valve as you can. Compressed air can blow water out of the pipes.
Wrap pipes you can’t drain, around their main valves, in blankets, house insulation or newspaper.
Disconnect a water softener so the hard and soft water pipes and its controls can drain.
Traps you can reach: take out the drain plugs or disconnect the traps. Traps you can’t reach: blow them out with compressed air, or use antifreeze as in Water in winter.
Also drain humidifiers and the refrigerator’s ice maker, and check sump pumps.

blocks.warn: Never put car antifreeze (ethylene glycol) in any part of a home water system (Purdue Extension).

blocks.p: Water heater: the power or gas must be off before you drain it (FEMA, in Water already in your house). An explosion could result if a water heater is left on without water in it (University of Wisconsin Extension).

list: If the heat will be off for several hours or more below freezing, keep exposed heating pipes from freezing (Purdue Extension).
If you still have power, keep the circulator pump running. If the room falls below 40°F (4°C), you should probably start draining the pipes (Purdue Extension).
Most hot-water heating systems are not easy to drain. Open the radiator vents to let air in so the pipes can drain (Purdue Extension).
Ask a heating contractor before adding antifreeze to the heating system (Purdue Extension).
Once it is drained, don’t fire the boiler again until the system is refilled (this app’s own caution): see Coming back.

blocks.p: Never drink the water from radiators or a hot-water boiler (FEMA): see Water already in your house.

list: Stored water: keep it in the warmest part of the house, above freezing. CDC says to store it at 50°F to 70°F (10°C to 21°C). Leave 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) of air at the top of anything that may freeze, and use plastic, not glass (Ohio State University Extension). Both are in Water in winter.
Canned food: don’t store cans in a damp garage or basement, or anywhere the temperature swings to extremes (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service).
A can that froze may swell. Never use a swollen can: throw it out (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service).
Throw out frozen cans that thawed at 40°F (4°C) or warmer, even if they are not swollen. Cans that thawed and froze again are not safe (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service).

blocks.p: No source opened says more than this about stored water in an unheated house.

blocks.warn: Signs the roof is overloaded: sagging roof framing or sheathing, sagging ceilings, popping, cracking and creaking noises, doors or windows that no longer open or close, cracked or split wood, cracks in walls or masonry, and severe roof leaks. If you see them, get everyone out at once, then have the local building authority or a qualified design professional inspect it (FEMA).

list: Don’t go up on the roof. Clear snow only from the ground, with a rake that is not metal (FEMA: snow removal only by qualified people; University of Minnesota Extension: contact professionals).
Snow removal is dangerous work for trained people (FEMA). Anyone on the roof in winter, or working on it from below, risks injury (University of Minnesota Extension).

From the ground, use a long-handled snow rake that is not metal, and stay well away from the eaves: roof snow can slide without warning. Metal rakes can damage the roof and carry a risk of electric shock (FEMA).
Leave at least a couple of inches (5 cm) of snow on the roof (FEMA).
Falling icicles can hurt people even from a short height (FEMA).

blocks.p: An ice dam is a ridge of ice at the edge of the roof that stops melting snow draining off. Water backs up behind it and can leak into the attic and the house. Heat escaping through the roof causes it (University of Minnesota Extension). Clearing snow off the roof takes away one of the things it needs (University of Minnesota Extension). If water has come in, dry the wet parts of the house right away to prevent mold (University of Minnesota Extension).

list: Before you turn the water back on or thaw a pipe, know where the main valve is: a pipe may already be broken and leak as it thaws. If it does, shut the main valve until it is repaired (Water in winter, from the Red Cross).
If one pipe froze, others may have too. Check every faucet (Red Cross).
If you can’t find the frozen part, can’t reach it or can’t thaw it, call a licensed plumber (Red Cross). Get an expert for plumbing repairs whenever you can (University of Wisconsin Extension).

Warm a frozen pipe only with gentle heat, such as an electric heating pad, a hair dryer, an electric space heater kept away from anything that can burn (plugged straight into a wall outlet: see Generators), or towels soaked in hot water, with the faucet open, until full pressure is back (Red Cross).
If pipes burst, stay out of standing water: you could get an electric shock (New York State Department of Health). Keep electric cords away from water (Water in winter).
Refill the water heater before you turn its power or gas back on (FEMA, in Water already in your house).

If you drained the hot-water heating system: no source opened covers this. This app’s own caution: don’t fire the boiler until the drained system has been refilled, and have a heating contractor refill and restart it (Purdue Extension also says to consult a heating contractor before adding antifreeze).
Getting the furnace going again: see Stay warm when the heat is out.
